Book: Materialist Tendencies in Arab-Islamic Philosophy (Volume II)

Anyone with a serious interest in Arab cultural life knows the historic intellectual importance of Husayn Muruwwa’s Materialist Tendencies in Arab-Islamic Philosophy. They also know the gap this book filled in the Arabic library, especially for democratic and progressive readers. Muruwwa intended it to be an encyclopedic work, useful to intellectuals in general and progressive intellectuals in particular, as well as university students and anyone interested in cultural questions more broadly.

But this enormous book was originally published by Dar al-Farabi in only two volumes. The first ran to more than a thousand pages, while the second reached around eight hundred. Edition followed edition, and the book gradually became an essential reference for intellectuals, researchers, and students at Arab universities.

Today, some readers may be interested only in the pre-Islamic period, for example. Others may care mainly about Muruwwa’s method, or about his materialist analysis of Ibn Sīnā’s philosophy, without needing the other sections. Buying only the part a reader needs also costs less than buying the entire work.
We have therefore decided to publish a new edition in four volumes:
Volume I: The methodological introduction, followed by studies of the pre-Islamic period and of the rise and early period of Islam.
Volume II: Kalām—the Muʿtazila and Ashʿarism—followed by Aristotelian formal logic, which the Muʿtazila were the first to use.
Volume III: Sufism, examined through two examples only: Ibn ʿArabī and al-Suhrawardī; the Epistles of the Brethren of Purity; and a brief account of the development of the sciences among the Arabs.
Volume IV: The mature stage of philosophy: al-Kindī, al-Fārābī, and Ibn Sīnā.
Historians usually date the beginning of the Umayyad period to 661 CE. But this date reflects an Islamic judgment more than a purely historical one.

Muʿāwiya ibn Abī Sufyān had already proclaimed himself caliph in 660 and received the oath of allegiance from the people of Syria. Yet ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib was still alive, and a large part of the Muslim population—in Iraq, the Hijaz, and other regions—continued to recognize ʿAlī as the fourth caliph.

In effect, historians have removed one year from the history of the Umayyad caliphate because most Muslims considered ʿAlī to be the legitimate caliph during that year. Muʿāwiya’s rule was accepted as an established reality only after the period of the four Rightly Guided Caliphs ended with ʿAlī’s death.

For one year of Islamic history, then, religious and political authority was divided between two caliphs at the same time: ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya. It was also divided between two capitals: Kufa, ʿAlī’s capital, and Damascus, Muʿāwiya’s.

One sign of Muʿāwiya’s political skill was his decision to proclaim himself caliph in Jerusalem. There stood Bayt al-Maqdis, or the al-Aqsa Mosque, which Muslims regarded as comparable to Mecca in sanctity. In the earliest period of Islam, Muslims had been instructed to face al-Aqsa during prayer. This was later changed, and they were instructed instead to face the Kaʿba in Mecca. For this reason, al-Aqsa is known among Muslims as “the first of the two prayer directions.”

Muʿāwiya wanted to give his caliphate a religious character. Since he could not use the Kaʿba for this purpose, he chose the place that held a corresponding sacred status in Muslim eyes. His immediate aim, at least, was to influence the Muslims of Syria, secure the Umayyad throne in its first stronghold, and then prepare the way for extending that authority throughout the other Muslim regions.

The Umayyad state became known for moving away from the Islamic principle of equality among peoples. The Qurʾān had declared, “The most honored of you in the sight of God is the most righteous of you” (Qurʾān 49:13), while the Prophet had said, “An Arab has no superiority over a non-Arab except through piety.”
In fact, the strong Arab partisanship that marked Umayyad policy through much of its history had already begun under Muʿāwiya ibn Abī Sufyān himself.

Given the circumstances in which Muʿāwiya established his state in the name of the “Islamic caliphate,” he had no reason to expect that his rule would quickly become secure throughout the whole Islamic world. At the moment when he declared himself caliph, the political struggle had become so intense that the new state faced serious threats from every direction.

Muʿāwiya could rely on little beyond the people of Syria, both Muslim and non-Muslim, to withstand these threats. From the way events looked at the time, several outcomes must have seemed possible to him. We have strong reason to think that one of the most important was the possibility that his state would remain confined to its original stronghold: Syria. At that time, the Syrian region included what are now Syria, Palestine, and Lebanon.
These circumstances forced Muʿāwiya to work on two fronts that may at first seem contradictory, though in reality they were not.

On one side, he built a close alliance with the original inhabitants of Syria, especially the Christians. On the other, he formed an equally strong alliance with the most powerful Arab tribes whose main branches lived there.

These were the Qaḥṭānī, or Kalbī, tribes. They belonged to one of the two broad ancestral groupings into which the Arab people were traditionally divided: the Qaḥṭānī or Kalbī group, associated with southern Arabia, and the ʿAdnānī or Qaysī group, associated with northern Arabia.
Most of the Arabs of Syria were Kalbīs. Some were Christians who had adopted Christianity during the period of Byzantine rule.

When the Arab conquest of the region took place, the conquering forces included Arabs from both major groupings, Kalbī and Qaysī. At that stage, the common aims of conquest prevented their older rivalries and loyalties from coming openly to the surface.

Because Muʿāwiya belonged to the Umayyad branch of Quraysh, we might have expected him to side with the Qaysīs, since Quraysh itself was Qaysī. But Muʿāwiya was a skilled politician. Tribal loyalty mattered to him only when it helped his political aims.
He therefore had little difficulty forming an alliance with the Kalbīs against the Qaysīs. Through this alliance, he could win the support of the different important forces in Syria.
He strengthened the alliance through marriage. He married Maymūna, a Kalbī woman, and later married their son Yazīd to another woman from the same tribal group.

By then, tribal rivalries had already begun to revive after the political struggle that erupted with the killing of ʿUthmān. Material conditions also played a part. The Kalbīs in Syria generally enjoyed better living conditions than the Qaysīs elsewhere, and this difference helped fuel jealousy and hostility between the two sides.
Muʿāwiya’s alliance with the Kalbīs gave the Qaysīs a further reason for resentment. The alliance included both Muslim and Christian Kalbīs in Syria.
From this point onward, the rivalry between these two major Arab groupings became less a spontaneous feature of tribal life and more an organized political force.

Muʿāwiya wanted to make the Arab population a basic source of support for both his own ambitions and those of the Umayyad aristocracy. His aim was to extend his new state into all the regions where Arabs had already established themselves, and both Kalbīs and Qaysīs could be found in most of those regions.

He understood that an alliance with the Kalbīs in Syria could help him win the support of Kalbīs wherever they lived. And the sharper the tribal struggle became between the two Arab groupings, the more strongly Kalbīs everywhere would rally around a ruler who had become their ally. His new state would itself become an important part of their strength against their Qaysī rivals.
Muʿāwiya eventually achieved what he wanted.
The Umayyad state he had founded moved beyond its original Syrian stronghold and soon became the sole Arab state for almost a century—eighty-nine years.

The Kalbīs remained one of its strongest sources of support. They even became the decisive force that saved the state from collapse after the death of Muʿāwiya II ibn Yazīd, the direct grandson of Muʿāwiya I.

At that point, the Umayyad state entered a crisis that nearly destroyed it. ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr claimed the caliphate for himself and won support among Muslims in the Hijaz and Iraq. The Qaysīs sided with him.

A fierce battle then broke out between the Qaysī and Kalbī tribes at Marj Rāhiṭ, near Damascus. The Kalbīs fought fiercely to defend the Umayyad state because their own interests were tied to it. They defeated their Qaysī opponents and restored the state’s strength.

But the result of the battle also transferred control of the Umayyad state from its founding family, the house of Muʿāwiya—the descendants of Abū Sufyān—to another branch of the Umayyads, the descendants of al-Ḥakam.
Immediately after the Battle of Marj Rāhiṭ, Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam took the Umayyad throne in Damascus. His branch of the family remained in power until the state finally fell.
Only three members of Muʿāwiya’s own line ruled the Umayyad state: Muʿāwiya himself, his son Yazīd, and his grandson Muʿāwiya ibn Yazīd.
3 — The Social System of the Umayyad State
We have seen that Muʿāwiya I relied on Arab tribes as a base of support for his rule.

Does this mean that the social system of the Umayyad state was itself based on tribal organization? Did Muʿāwiya turn society backward, restoring the tribal system that we saw already beginning to break apart even before Islam?
History cannot simply be turned backward by objective conditions. How, then, could it be turned backward by one person’s will?
In fact, Muʿāwiya had no such intention anyway. He was founding a state, and the creation of a state was itself historically more advanced than tribal organization.

The state he founded also met a historical need that had emerged as class divisions developed within society. A state required stability and accumulation, and both stood in a close, changing relationship with wider social development.
The conditions for this already existed in Syria when the Arabs conquered it.

By the time Muʿāwiya became governor there, the old natural economy had already been breaking down for a long time. New economic relationships were taking its place, not only in Syria but also in Mesopotamia and other parts of the eastern region.
Centers of exchange had appeared. At first they drew in local trade, then gradually expanded to serve a much wider region.
Historical development had therefore already moved a long way toward a social and economic system that went beyond the old natural economy.

Under Muʿāwiya, first as governor and then as caliph, the most important feature of this system across the region was its feudal character, combined with a strong military structure. This was a continuation of patterns that had developed under Byzantine and Sasanian rule.
Earlier, when discussing the caliphate of ʿUthmān, we saw how the Umayyad governors he appointed in the provinces quickly became landowners.

They had originally entered these regions not only as conquerors, but also as bearers of a new message that appealed to local people by promising an end to the oppression of their previous rulers. Once the new governors moved beyond that role and began acquiring land and wealth for themselves, the result was a social revolt that eventually led to the killing of the caliph himself.
The conduct of these Arab governors was not simply a matter of individual choices. It reflected their social and class position, but there were also objective historical forces at work.

Before the Arab-Islamic conquest, a particular form of military feudal relations had already developed in Syria and Mesopotamia. This had become the dominant feature of the social system in those regions.
That existing system inevitably influenced the form taken by Arab rule after the conquest, especially once Syria entered a period of stability under Muʿāwiya, first as governor and later as caliph.

The Umayyad ruling class also had a direct interest in making as much use as possible of a system whose roots and dominant relations of production were already firmly established. They therefore pushed further in the same direction, strengthening and deepening its foundations.
Their class interest had a very concrete basis.

Muʿāwiya and his family came into possession of large areas of land that had belonged before the Arab-Islamic conquest to the Byzantine emperor and the Byzantine aristocracy. Under the Islamic system of landholding, these lands should have become public property belonging to the Islamic state.
Instead, under Muʿāwiya and his relatives and close associates, they became private property.

Muʿāwiya employed Syrian experts to organize farming and irrigation on these lands. He and his closest relatives and supporters soon became some of the largest landowners in the region. Together they formed a new, semi-feudal aristocracy after the conquest.

Meanwhile, most other Arabs were occupied with military campaigns in distant regions or stationed in military camps to defend the state against uprisings and to fight political movements opposed to Umayyad rule in Iraq and elsewhere.
These conditions of conquest and internal political conflict gradually created certain habits among the Arabs.
One was their contempt for agricultural and craft work. The circumstances of conquest had left much of this work to slaves and to the original inhabitants of the conquered regions.

Together with surviving tribal traditions, these habits encouraged a sense of superiority over non-Arabs. The Umayyad state itself adopted this attitude and referred to non-Arabs as mawālī, or clients.
Under Umayyad rule, then, anyone who was not Arab could be described as a mawlā.
This kind of discrimination became one of the forces that helped destroy the Umayyad state before it had even completed a full century of existence.
When Muʿāwiya helped revive tribal loyalties early in his rule, however, he did not originally intend to make discrimination of this kind a permanent principle of Umayyad government.

His purpose at that stage was more immediate. He wanted to use the rivalry between the Qaysīs and Kalbīs to strengthen a throne that still faced serious danger after the caliphate had moved away from the political foundations of the Rightly Guided period.

The Umayyad caliphs who came after him went much further. They emphasized Arab privilege so strongly that they provoked resentment among the non-Arab populations of their state and encouraged an opposing form of ethnic hostility.

That counter-hostility later helped produce the movement that appeared toward the end of Umayyad rule and continued to develop under the Abbasids until it became hostile to the Arab people themselves, as well as to their history and culture.
Its hostility toward everything Arab eventually created an intellectual current that attacked Arab literature, thought, values, and traditions. This was the well-known Shuʿūbiyya movement.

In discussing the social system of the Umayyad period, we should also mention something else Muʿāwiya achieved as caliph: he gave the emerging Arab state a more concrete and developed administrative structure, helping turn it into a new feature of Arab civilization.

He established various dīwāns, which performed some of the functions that government departments or ministries perform today. There were offices for taxation and customs duties, accounts, official correspondence, the judiciary, and other areas of government.
At first, however, some of these offices kept their records in local languages: Persian in Iran and Iraq, Greek in Syria, and Coptic in Egypt.
The currency in circulation also remained much as it had been before the Arab conquest until the reigns of ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān and al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik.
